title: Twisted Multilayer Graphene: Superperiodicity and quasicrystals
abstract: This thesis investigates how superperiodicity, quasiperiodicity, and disorder shape electronic and spin transport in graphene-based systems, with an emphasis on experimentally relevant length scales and realistic atomistic modeling. Using large-scale real-space quantum-transport methods, it first establishes controlled transport fingerprints that distinguish conventional Bloch propagation in periodic structures from the anomalous dynamics induced by quasiperiodic modulations. Building on this framework, the thesis analyzes magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and shows that, within a finite disorder window where flat-band features remain robust, moderate Anderson disorder can counterintuitively enhance the mean free path. This disorder-induced delocalization is further linked to changes in the quantum metric extracted from optical conductivity, revealing a direct connection between transport, electronic geometry, and the real-space extent of the underlying states. The study then turns to graphene quasicrystal approximants and hybrid multilayer stacks, identifying sub-ballistic transport and self-similar localization patterns as signatures of quasicrystalline order, while also demonstrating their strong fragility against disorder and interlayer proximity effects. Finally, the thesis addresses spin transport in suspended monolayer graphene, showing that atomic-scale corrugations generate short-range fluctuating Rashba fields that can limit spin lifetimes to the nanosecond range even when charge transport remains close to ballistic. Taken together, these results provide a unified picture of how geometry, disorder, and structural complexity govern transport phenomena in twisted and corrugated graphene systems.
summary: This thesis comprehensively analyzes electronic and spin transport in complex graphene structures exhibiting super- or quasiperiodicity. It demonstrates that disorder can paradoxically enhance conductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene while identifying unique signatures of quasicrystalline order. Overall, it unifies the understanding of how geometry and structural imperfections govern quantum transport phenomena.
main_problem: The study investigates how structural complexities like superperiodicity, quasiperiodicity, and disorder fundamentally shape electronic and spin transport in graphene-based materials.
main_result: The work establishes that moderate disorder can counterintuitively enhance the mean free path in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, while quasicrystalline order exhibits distinct sub-ballistic localization signatures fragile to structural perturbations.
method: The research employs large-scale real-space quantum-transport methods, utilizing Kubo-type formulations and tight-binding descriptions incorporating curvature effects.
model_or_system: The primary systems studied are graphene, specifically in its twisted multilayer form (including magic-angle interfaces), quasicrystal approximants, and suspended monolayer sheets for spin transport analysis.
key_observables: Mean free path, quantum metric derived from optical conductivity, sub-ballistic exponent, and spin lifetimes.
important_parameters: Disorder strength (Anderson disorder), structural periodicity (super/quasiperiodicity), and interlayer proximity effects.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on established transport formalisms and assumes that flat-band features remain robust enough to exhibit specific disorder-induced delocalization behavior.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the work builds upon establishing controlled transport fingerprints distinguishing various periodic modulations.
paper_structure: The thesis progresses from fundamental concepts (superperiodicity/quasiperiodicity) to computational methods, analyzing controlled models, then focusing sequentially on disorder effects in twisted multilayer graphene and spin transport in corrugated monolayer systems.
why_interesting: It provides a detailed framework for understanding how geometric frustration and randomness interact with quantum coherence, which is central to open quantum system dynamics and localization studies.
